strengths: The method addresses a practically important problem: distilling high-resolution image datasets without expensive bilevel optimization. Combining representative teacher features with per-class BatchNorm regularization is intuitive and potentially useful.

The reported improvements are substantial. At 50 images per class, WMDD achieves 57.6% on ImageNet-1K versus 53.5% for the strongest listed baseline, and 59.4% on Tiny ImageNet versus 48.7% (Table 1).

Evaluation covers several dataset sizes and image budgets, cross-architecture transfer to ResNets and vision transformers, component ablations, regularization sensitivity, and sliced Wasserstein alternatives. Table 4 supports the effectiveness of combining feature matching with PCBN.

The manuscript provides pseudocode, implementation settings, repeated-run uncertainty, and a code link. It credits the datasets, optimal-transport machinery, and preceding distillation frameworks, and acknowledges that distillation can preserve source-data biases.
weaknesses: The central objective needs clearer positioning relative to classical quantization. With one input distribution, squared Euclidean cost, and freely optimized support weights, Eq. (5) reduces to the k-means objective: min_B (1/n) sum_i min_j ||z_i-b_j||^2. The paper neither discusses this equivalence nor compares against k-means feature targets with the same reconstruction and PCBN pipeline. This leaves the claimed originality and necessity of the barycenter solver insufficiently established.

The experiments do not cleanly isolate the claimed advantage over MMD. Section 5.6 retains different feature-extractor setups—one pretrained teacher versus randomly initialized networks—even after removing augmentation and FKD. At one image per class, squared Wasserstein quantization and linear-MMD matching target the same feature mean under a shared encoder, so Figure 4's large difference cannot establish a metric advantage alone. Matched encoder, regularization, and training controls are needed.

The relationship between the headline comparisons and controlled ablations is unclear. On ImageNet-1K at 10 images per class, the CE+BN variant obtains 35.9% in Table 4, whereas SRe2L obtains 21.3% in Table 1 despite using the same basic objectives. The gain from replacing CE with Wasserstein matching under PCBN is 1.7 points. These are useful improvements, but the manuscript should reconcile the much larger baseline discrepancy and identify the effects of teacher training, recovery settings, and relabeling.

Algorithm 2 has an unresolved consistency issue: it computes a transport plan, updates its target weights, and then reuses that plan for the position update, although the derivation requires the plan's column sums to equal the current weights. Simplex projection also permits zero weights, making the inverse-weight update undefined. The initialization, barycenter learning rate, zero-weight handling, and precise use of sample weights in FKD are not sufficiently specified to assess or reproduce this component.

Appendix B supplies standard loss-discrepancy bounds but does not establish a tighter Wasserstein bound or connect teacher-feature quantization and image reconstruction to the performance of subsequently trained architectures. Its claim that characteristic-kernel MMD necessarily requires prohibitive quadratic computation also overlooks caching the constant real–real term and using stochastic estimators. The theoretical discussion therefore provides limited support for the proposed explanation.

Evidence for large-scale efficiency is less complete than the accuracy evidence. Table 3 measures ImageNette at one image per class, where the barycenter reduces to a mean; Table 5 adds Tiny ImageNet timings. An ImageNet-1K breakdown covering teacher training, feature extraction, transport, image recovery, and FKD time/storage is needed to substantiate the broader computational-savings claims.
